title: Halves your risk: from what?
hook: A pill "halves your risk". How many people does that actually spare?

knows: a risk written as a number of cases per 1,000 people
doesNotKnow: that a relative cut means little without the starting risk
the difference between a relative and an absolute reduction

misconception: "Halves your risk" means half of the people (or a large number) who would be harmed are spared.
objective: The learner can explain that halving a risk of 2 in 1,000 spares 1 person in 1,000, while the same halving at 200 in 1,000 spares 100: a relative cut is a share of the starting risk.
keyState: Pill on at 2 in 1,000 (cases 2 -> 1, spared 1), then pill on at 200 in 1,000 (spared 100).

claims.text: At a risk of 2 in 1,000, 2 of 1,000 people get the condition; a pill that halves the risk leaves 1, so it spares 1 person in 1,000.
At 2 in 1,000 the halving lowers the risk by 1 in 1,000, so 1,000 people take the pill for one to be spared.
claims.source: Absolute risk reduction 0.002 - 0.001 = 0.001 (0.1 percentage points); number needed to treat = 1 / 0.001 = 1,000.

claims.text: At 20 in 1,000 halving spares 10; at 200 in 1,000 the same halving spares 100.
A relative cut is a share of the starting risk, so the same "halves your risk" can spare 1 person or 100 per 1,000.
claims.source: Relative risk reduction = (baseline - treated) / baseline = 50% at every baseline on the stage, while the absolute reduction is baseline / 2.

claims.text: The pill is made up; the arithmetic is the same for any treatment.
claims.source: Hypothetical example; no real drug or trial is described. Which dots are red is a seeded shuffle (LAYOUT_SEED 2024, layout only; counts are exact and do not depend on the seed).

recall.question: A screening test "cuts deaths by 25%", from 4 in 1,000 to 3 in 1,000. Out of 1,000 people screened, how many deaths does it prevent?
recall.why: The cut is 25% of the starting risk of 4 in 1,000: 4 - 3 = 1 death prevented per 1,000 people screened.
